title: A MAN COULD BE UNCLEAN UNTIL EVENING AFTER A BODILY EMISSION—BUT DID GOD REALLY CALL HIM A SINNER?
paragraphs: A MAN COULD BE UNCLEAN UNTIL EVENING AFTER A BODILY EMISSION—BUT DID GOD REALLY CALL HIM A SINNER?

Leviticus 15:16–18 reveals a truth many Christians have never been taught: Not everything that made someone ceremonially unclean was morally sinful. And when you finally understand the difference, you may never read the Law of Moses—or the cleansing power of Jesus Christ—the same way again.
There are Bible verses people read aloud in church.
And then there are Bible verses people quietly skip.
Not because they are unimportant.
But because they make us uncomfortable.

They mention things we would rather not discuss. Things involving our bodies. Our sexuality. Our private lives. Things that seem too personal, too strange, or too embarrassing to belong in a holy book.
And somewhere in the middle of those uncomfortable passages is a command that has left countless readers confused.
A man experiences an emission of semen.
He washes.
He remains unclean until evening.
And suddenly, a question rises that many believers have been afraid to ask:
Did God consider a man sinful simply because his body functioned the way God designed it to function?
Read that question again.
Because the answer matters more than you might think.
It matters to the young Christian struggling to distinguish temptation from sin.
It matters to the married couple who wonders whether physical intimacy somehow diminishes their holiness.
It matters to the believer carrying years of unnecessary shame over ordinary bodily experiences.
And it matters to anyone who has ever mistaken the language of ritual uncleanness for the verdict of moral condemnation.
Here is what makes this passage so remarkable.
God commanded cleansing even when the passage did not identify a moral offense.
And if you do not understand why, you may misunderstand not only Leviticus, but the very holiness of God, the purpose of His Law, and the astonishing beauty of what Jesus Christ came to accomplish.
The answer begins in a place most modern readers would never expect.
Ancient Israel.
A wilderness camp.
A holy God dwelling among His people.
And a command about something as ordinary as the human body.
Leviticus 15:16–18 says in the King James Version:
“And if any man's seed of copulation go out from him, then he shall wash all his flesh in water, and be unclean until the even.
And every garment, and every skin, whereon is the seed of copulation, shall be washed with water, and be unclean until the even.
The woman also with whom man shall lie with seed of copulation, they shall both bathe themselves in water, and be unclean until the even.”
There it is.
No attempt to hide it.
No embarrassed apology from Scripture.
No suggestion that the human body is too shameful for God's attention.
The Lord who created the heavens and the earth was also concerned with the ordinary physical realities of the people He had redeemed.
But notice something that changes the entire conversation.
The passage says unclean.
It does not say guilty of sexual immorality.
It does not call the emission itself an act of rebellion.
It does not instruct the man to confess this ordinary bodily event as a moral transgression.
And in verses 16–18, it does not require a sin offering.
That distinction is not a small theological technicality.
It is the doorway into understanding what this passage actually means.
The Hebrew word translated “unclean” is טָמֵא (ṭāmēʾ).
In the context of Leviticus, this word frequently describes a condition of ritual impurity.
Its meaning must be understood within the ceremonial system God gave Israel.
It is not automatically equivalent to the Hebrew vocabulary for sin, such as חֵטְא (ḥēṭʾ), a term associated with sin or offense.
Those words are not interchangeable.
And neither are the realities they describe.
A person could become ritually unclean through circumstances that did not necessarily involve moral wrongdoing.
Contact with a dead body could produce impurity.
Childbirth involved a period of ritual purification.
Menstruation involved ritual impurity.
Certain skin conditions could make someone ceremonially unclean.
And the normal emission of semen could do the same.
Does that mean childbirth was sinful?
No.
Does that mean menstruation was a moral offense?
No.
Does that mean touching the dead was always an act of wickedness?
No.
In fact, the same Law that regulated contact with death also commanded Israelites to honor their parents.
Ritual impurity and personal sin could sometimes overlap, but they were not identical categories.
That is where so many misunderstandings begin.
We read the word “unclean” through modern emotional associations.
We hear “dirty.”
We imagine “disgusting.”
We assume “sinful.”
And before we know it, we have turned a ceremonial condition into a moral accusation that the passage itself never makes.
But the Hebrew text invites us to read more carefully.
In Leviticus 15:16, the expression שִׁכְבַת־זָרַע (shikhvat-zeraʿ) refers to an emission or discharge of semen.
The command that follows is וְרָחַץ (wĕrāḥaṣ), meaning “and he shall wash” or “bathe.”
Then comes the phrase וְטָמֵא עַד־הָעָרֶב (wĕṭāmēʾ ʿad-hāʿārev).
“And he shall be unclean until evening.”
Not forever.
Not until he earns forgiveness through suffering.
Not until he proves he is worthy of being loved.
Until evening.
A defined period within Israel's ritual system.
The instruction was not a declaration that the body was evil.
It was part of a larger pattern through which Israel learned to distinguish the holy from the common, and the clean from the unclean.
Leviticus 10:10 explicitly speaks of distinguishing between what is holy and common, and between what is unclean and clean.
These distinctions taught Israel how to live in the presence of the Lord.
And this is where the story becomes deeper.
Because Leviticus was not written to a people trying to invent their own way to reach God.
It was given to a people God had already rescued.
Israel had been brought out of Egypt.
Delivered from slavery.
Led through the wilderness.
And called into covenant fellowship with the God who had redeemed them.
At the center of their camp stood the tabernacle.
The dwelling place associated with God's holy presence among His people.
And that presence changed everything.
The issue was not that ordinary human biology had suddenly become wicked.
The issue was that Israel was being taught that approaching the holy God was not something to treat casually.
Leviticus 15:31 reveals the seriousness of the system:
“Thus shall ye separate the children of Israel from their uncleanness; that they die not in their uncleanness, when they defile my tabernacle that is among them.” — KJV
Now the broader picture becomes clearer.
These regulations were connected to the holiness of God's dwelling among His people.
They governed ceremonial purity, access to sacred space, and the preservation of distinctions that mattered within Israel's covenant life.
Many scholars also recognize that the impurity regulations frequently involve bodily conditions associated with life, reproduction, mortality, and the fragility of human existence.
That observation can help explain the pattern, but Scripture does not explicitly tell us that every individual purity law was established for one single symbolic reason.
We should not pretend to know more than the text reveals.
What we can say confidently is this:
Ritual uncleanness was a real covenantal condition under the Mosaic Law, but it was not always evidence of personal sin.
And that changes how we read the next verse.
Leviticus 15:18 speaks about a man and woman having sexual intercourse and afterward bathing and remaining unclean until evening.
Think carefully about what that means.
The text does not restrict the regulation to an adulterous relationship.
It does not identify marital intimacy itself as a violation of God's moral law.
The wider witness of Scripture makes clear that marriage and its physical union are not inherently sinful.
Genesis 2:24 describes a man and his wife becoming one flesh.
Genesis 1:28 presents fruitfulness as part of God's blessing upon humanity.
Hebrews 13:4 declares:
“Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled...” — KJV
So how could a married couple experience ritual uncleanness after an act that was not itself morally forbidden?
Because ceremonial uncleanness did not necessarily mean moral guilt.
That is the answer.
Not an excuse.
Not an attempt to soften Scripture.
Not a modern reinterpretation designed to make God's commandments more comfortable.
It is a distinction arising from the text itself.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs to hear that with particular care.
Your body is not automatically your enemy.
Your humanity is not automatically a scandal.
A physical response is not, by itself, proof that you have committed a moral offense.
God created human beings as embodied creatures.
And the Bible does not require us to hate the bodies He made.
But please do not misunderstand this truth.
It does not mean every sexual thought, desire, intention, or action is morally innocent.
Jesus spoke seriously about lustful intent in Matthew 5:27–28.
Scripture consistently condemns sexual immorality.
And the Christian call to holiness includes our minds, desires, relationships, and bodies.
An involuntary bodily emission is not the same thing as deliberately cultivating lust.
Ordinary marital intimacy is not the same thing as adultery.
A physical condition is not the same thing as a chosen act of disobedience.
And the fact that an act involved the body does not, by itself, determine whether it was sinful.
The moral question must be answered by what God actually commands and forbids, not merely by whether a bodily function makes us uncomfortable.
This is especially important because shame can become a terrible spiritual teacher.
Shame does not always tell the truth.
Sometimes it accuses where Scripture has not accused.
Sometimes it silences questions that deserve careful biblical answers.
Sometimes it convinces a believer that holiness means feeling disgusted with being human.
And sometimes it hides genuine sin beneath the very confusion it creates.
That is why we need the Word of God rather than our assumptions.
Because one person may need to stop condemning himself for something Scripture has not called sin.
Another may need to stop using that distinction to excuse lust, exploitation, or disobedience.
Both need truth.
Both need grace.
Both need Jesus Christ.
And neither is helped by twisting the Bible.
There is another important detail in Leviticus 15 that deserves our attention.
The chapter distinguishes ordinary emissions from an abnormal bodily discharge.
Earlier, in Leviticus 15:2–15, the text addresses a man with a continuing discharge.
The purification process is more extensive, and after the discharge ends, offerings are required, including a sin offering and a burnt offering.
That might surprise you.
Does the presence of a sin offering mean every bodily discharge was a moral offense?
Not necessarily.
In Leviticus, the Hebrew term חַטָּאת (ḥaṭṭāʾt), traditionally translated “sin offering,” can also be understood in sacrificial contexts as a purification offering.
Such offerings could address ritual impurity and its consequences for sacred space, not merely deliberate moral wrongdoing.
Leviticus 12, concerning purification after childbirth, provides another important example.
The fact that a purification offering was required does not mean giving birth was a sin.
This is why context matters.
This is why the details matter.
This is why pulling one uncomfortable verse out of its covenant setting can produce an entire theology that God never intended.
And this is also why Leviticus should never be treated as a book of meaningless ancient restrictions.
Its laws were part of a serious, holy system.
They revealed that God's presence was not ordinary.
They taught Israel that impurity could not simply be ignored in the worship life of the covenant community.
They established boundaries around the tabernacle.
And within the unfolding story of Scripture, they prepare us to appreciate the greater cleansing revealed through Jesus Christ.
But before we arrive at the cross, there is a scene in the Gospels that I want you to imagine.
A woman is walking through a crowd.
For twelve years, she has suffered from bleeding.
Twelve years.
Not twelve days.
Not twelve weeks.
Twelve years of suffering.
Mark 5:25–34 tells us that she had endured much under many physicians, spent what she had, and grown worse rather than better.
And under the purity regulations of Leviticus 15:25–30, a prolonged abnormal flow of blood had serious ritual implications.
Imagine what that could mean for her daily life.
The physical weakness.
The uncertainty.
The cost.
The limitations.
The emotional burden of living with a condition that affected her participation in the religious and social world around her.
We should not invent details about how every person treated her, because the Gospel does not tell us everything.
But we do know she was desperate.
And we know she had heard about Jesus.
So she approached Him in the crowd.
And she touched His garment.
Not because she had a sophisticated theological explanation for everything that was happening.
But because she believed He could heal her.
Mark 5:28 records her thought:
“If I may touch but his clothes, I shall be whole.” — KJV
And immediately, the bleeding stopped.
Jesus knew that power had gone out from Him.
He turned and asked who had touched His clothes.
The woman came forward, trembling.
She fell before Him.
And told Him the truth.
Can you picture that moment?
A suffering woman.
A surrounding crowd.
A condition that had consumed twelve years of her life.
And Jesus looking directly at her.
He did not dismiss her.
He did not call her disgusting.
He did not treat her suffering as proof that she was morally corrupt.
He said:
“Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace, and be whole of thy plague.” — Mark 5:34, KJV
Daughter.
What a word.
Not an anonymous problem.
Not an inconvenience.
Not merely a body with a medical condition.
Daughter.
And here is the astonishing contrast.
Under the Mosaic purity system, contact with certain sources of impurity ordinarily required cleansing.
But in this Gospel account, Jesus does not become powerless before her condition.
His healing power overcomes it.
The woman who had suffered for twelve years leaves restored.
We must not misread this scene as though the Law of Moses were evil or as though Jesus despised the holiness that Law taught.
Jesus did not come to celebrate impurity or dismiss God's holiness.
He came as the fulfillment of God's redemptive purposes.
Matthew 5:17 records His own words:
“Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil.” — KJV
That word “fulfil” matters.
In the Greek text, the verb is πληρῶσαι (plērōsai), from πληρόω (plēroō), meaning to fulfill or bring to completion.
Jesus did not announce that God's holiness had become irrelevant.
He revealed the fulfillment toward which the Scriptures pointed.
The Law exposed humanity's need for holiness, purification, and reconciliation with God.
The sacrificial system revealed the seriousness of approaching the Lord.
And Jesus came to accomplish what the old covenant sacrifices could never finally accomplish.
Hebrews 10:1 teaches that the Law possessed a shadow of the good things to come rather than their complete reality.
Hebrews 10:4 says:
“For it is not possible that the blood of bulls and of goats should take away sins.” — KJV
Then Hebrews directs our eyes toward Jesus Christ.
The One who offered Himself.
The One whose sacrifice does not need endless repetition.
The One through whom sinners can receive forgiveness and access to God.
And suddenly, the discussion is no longer only about a man washing after a bodily emission.
It is about the greater question every human being must eventually face.
How can an unholy sinner be reconciled to a holy God?
That is a different question from whether a natural emission is itself sinful.
But it is the question toward which the larger biblical story leads.
Because even if a man could become ceremonially clean by evening under the Law of Moses, that did not mean he had been made morally perfect.
And even if someone had never experienced the particular impurity described in Leviticus 15, that would not mean he was free from sin.
Romans 3:23 says:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” — KJV
All.
Not merely those whose bodies experienced ritual impurity.
Not merely those who violated ceremonial regulations.
All have sinned.
The human problem runs deeper than physical conditions.
It reaches the heart.
Our pride.
Our deceit.
Our selfishness.
Our lust.
Our cruelty.
Our refusal to love God with all that we are.
Our attempts to appear righteous while concealing what we know is wrong.
We can wash our skin and still harbor hatred.
We can wear clean clothes and still speak lies.
We can look respectable in church and still carry a heart unwilling to surrender to God.
That is why Jesus taught that moral defilement comes from the evil that proceeds from within the human heart.
In Mark 7:20–23, He identifies sins such as evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, greed, deceit, and pride.
The distinction is profound.
A physical emission did not automatically make someone guilty of those sins.
And outward cleanliness could never guarantee freedom from them.
Jesus was confronting a deeper problem.
Not the existence of human bodies.
The corruption of human hearts.
And now consider how often we reverse those priorities.
We become obsessed with appearances.
We panic over things God has not condemned.
Yet we quietly tolerate bitterness.
We excuse dishonesty.
We feed resentment.
We nurse secret pride.
We criticize someone else's visible struggle while refusing to confront our own hidden disobedience.
And sometimes, the person who feels most ashamed is not the person who has committed the gravest offense.
Sometimes the believer overwhelmed by guilt is someone who desperately wants to honor God but has never been taught how to distinguish biblical conviction from unnecessary shame.
If that describes you, listen carefully.
You do not need to manufacture guilt to prove you take holiness seriously.
And you do not need to deny real sin to believe that God's grace is sufficient.
True repentance begins with agreeing with God about what sin actually is.
Not adding accusations He never made.
Not removing commandments He clearly gave.
Agreeing with Him.
That means studying His Word carefully.
It means letting Scripture correct our assumptions.
It means refusing to build doctrine out of embarrassment.
And it means remembering that Jesus Christ did not come merely to make religious people feel more comfortable.
He came to save sinners.
That salvation was costly.
There was nothing casual about Calvary.
The Son of God was betrayed.
Rejected.
Mocked.
Scourged.
Crucified.
He bore our sins in His body on the tree, as 1 Peter 2:24 declares.
He suffered, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring us to God, as 1 Peter 3:18 teaches.
And He rose from the dead.
The empty tomb is not an inspiring metaphor.
It is central to the Christian proclamation that Jesus Christ has conquered death.
The Gospel is not that our bodies were never subject to weakness.
The Gospel is that the crucified and risen Christ offers forgiveness, reconciliation, and the promise of resurrection life.
And this brings us to a Greek word that beautifully expresses what God does for His people.
καθαρίζω (katharizō).
To cleanse.
To make clean.
It is used in the New Testament for different kinds of cleansing, including the cleansing of sin.
In 1 John 1:9, Scripture says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — KJV
The Greek expression καθαρίσῃ ἡμᾶς (katharisē hēmas) means “cleanse us.”
Notice what John is talking about.
Not simply washing the body after a ceremonial condition.
But cleansing from unrighteousness.
Forgiveness for genuine sin.
Restoration through the faithfulness and righteousness of God.
The kind of cleansing no ordinary bath could accomplish.
And this is why the Gospel is so precious.
Because there are things we have done that cannot be undone by washing our hands.
Words we cannot pull back.
Betrayals we cannot erase.
Choices whose consequences still hurt.
Sins we wish we could remove from the pages of our lives.
There are people reading this who know exactly what that feels like.
You remember the conversation.
The hidden compromise.
The moment you knew better and did it anyway.
The promise you broke.
The person you wounded.
The truth you concealed.
And maybe you have spent years trying to become a different person while secretly wondering whether God still sees the old you.
But hear what the Gospel announces.
Forgiveness is not purchased by pretending the sin never happened.
It is received through Jesus Christ, who died for sinners and rose again.
Grace does not declare evil to be good.
Grace provides mercy for the guilty through the Savior who bore sin.
And repentance does not mean earning your way back into God's favor.
It means turning from sin toward the Lord whose mercy is offered through Christ.
You cannot cleanse your conscience by punishing yourself endlessly.
You cannot purchase forgiveness with religious performance.
You cannot rewrite yesterday by pretending it did not happen.
But Jesus Christ is able to forgive and transform those who come to Him.
That is not permission to continue in sin.
Romans 6:1–2 explicitly rejects that idea.
It is an invitation to leave sin behind because grace has opened the way to a new life.
And perhaps this is where the message becomes personal.
Maybe your scandal was public.
People know what happened.
They remember.
They still talk.
Maybe your scandal was private.
Nobody knows what you did.
Nobody knows what you have been fighting.
You have learned how to smile through worship while carrying the weight of something unresolved.
Or maybe your struggle is different.
Maybe you have been carrying shame over something that was never sinful in the first place.
You were never taught the difference between involuntary bodily processes and deliberate moral choices.
You were taught to fear your own humanity rather than submit your whole humanity to the wisdom of God.
And the confusion has followed you into prayer.
Into marriage.
Into your understanding of holiness.
Into the way you imagine God looking at you.
Whatever your situation, the answer is not to make the Bible say what you want it to say.
The answer is to let the Bible speak.
Let Leviticus teach what ritual impurity meant within Israel's covenant.
Let Jesus teach what truly defiles the heart.
Let the apostles proclaim the forgiveness purchased through His blood.
And let the Holy Spirit use the truth to bring conviction where repentance is needed and freedom where false guilt has taken root.
Because not every uncomfortable feeling is the conviction of the Holy Spirit.
And not every comfortable feeling is evidence that we are walking in obedience.
We need something more reliable than either.
We need God's Word.
This is why 2 Timothy 2:15 calls believers to handle the word of truth rightly.
And it is why the distinction in Leviticus 15 matters so much.
When we confuse ritual impurity with moral sin, we risk placing burdens on consciences that Scripture itself does not place there.
When we erase the reality of moral sin, we risk withholding the very truth that leads us to repentance.
Neither error honors Christ.
Biblical faithfulness requires both holiness and mercy.
Truth and grace.
Conviction and compassion.
And at the center of it all stands Jesus Christ.
Not a Savior who tells us that sin is imaginary.
Not a Savior who despises the human body.
But the eternal Son of God who truly took on human flesh, lived without sin, died for our transgressions, and rose in victory.
The One who touched lepers.
The One who healed the bleeding woman.
The One who forgave sinners.
The One who called people to repentance.
The One who welcomed the weary.
The One who warned the self-righteous.
The One who laid down His life for His sheep.
And the One who still calls us to follow Him.
There is something else about Leviticus 15 that should remain with us.
The man who experienced an ordinary emission did not remain ritually unclean indefinitely.
The text repeatedly says:
Until evening.
A boundary.
A prescribed period.
An appointed conclusion.
We should not turn that phrase into a promise that every earthly hardship will end by tomorrow or that every sin is automatically forgiven after a period of waiting.
That would go beyond the passage.
But we can recognize the difference between the temporary ceremonial condition described there and the lasting reconciliation accomplished through Christ.
The Christian's confidence is not that every spiritual problem disappears when the sun goes down.
It is that Jesus Christ has offered the once-for-all sacrifice that the old covenant system could never provide.
Hebrews 10:14 declares:
“For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.” — KJV
One offering.
One sufficient Savior.
One Gospel.
And for those who belong to Christ, a hope that does not depend on endlessly repeating sacrifices to secure forgiveness.
That is the glory of the new covenant.
And it is why the old covenant purity laws deserve careful study rather than careless dismissal.
They are part of the story that helps us understand the holiness of God and the greatness of our Redeemer.
So the next time someone asks you whether Leviticus 15:16–18 means a man sinned simply because he experienced an emission of semen, you can answer with biblical clarity.
No. The passage describes ritual uncleanness under the Mosaic Law, not an automatic declaration of moral sin.
Its application to intercourse likewise does not make lawful marital intimacy sinful.
The distinction does not abolish biblical sexual ethics.
It helps us understand them more accurately.
And Christians today are not commanded to observe the old covenant ritual washing and evening-impurity regulations as the means of maintaining access to God.
The New Testament presents Jesus Christ as the fulfillment of the Law's redemptive purposes and the mediator of the new covenant.
We still pursue holiness.
We still flee sexual immorality.
We still honor God with our bodies.
But we do not treat ordinary bodily emissions as though they automatically constitute moral rebellion against Him.
That is not biblical holiness.
That is confusion.
And confusion is not the same thing as conviction.
Now I want to ask you something more personal than a question about ancient Israel.
What have you been calling sin that God has not called sin?
And what have you been excusing that God has clearly told you to surrender?
Those are two very different questions.
But both require the same kind of courage.
The courage to stand before the Word of God without hiding.
Without bargaining.
Without twisting the text to protect our preferences.
Without accepting unnecessary condemnation.
Perhaps today you need to release a burden of false guilt.
Perhaps today you need to confess a real sin.
Perhaps you need to apologize to someone.
Perhaps you need to seek wise pastoral guidance because years of confusion have left you afraid of your own body.
Perhaps you need to open your Bible again and discover that God's holiness is more beautiful, more serious, and more gracious than you once imagined.
Wherever you are, do not run away from Jesus.
Run toward Him.
Not because you have already made yourself clean.
But because He is the Savior who can forgive and restore.
You do not have to publish the details of your struggle.
You do not owe strangers your private history.
But you may find encouragement in knowing that other believers are learning, repenting, healing, and growing alongside you.
Your words may encourage someone who has been silently asking the same questions for years.
And if someone came to mind while you were reading, do not ignore that thought.
Maybe it is a young believer who has been terrified of asking questions about the Bible and the body.
Maybe it is a married couple who needs a clearer understanding of God's design for intimacy.
Maybe it is a friend who has quietly walked away from Christianity because the only version of holiness they ever encountered was shame without understanding.
Send this article to them.
Or send it privately with a simple message:
“I thought this might help you understand something important about Scripture.”
Not because social media engagement earns spiritual favor.
But because sound biblical teaching deserves to travel farther than confusion.
A single thoughtful share can place the truth of Scripture in front of someone who might never have searched for it.
Come back to the Hebrew words.
Read Leviticus 15 in its full context.
Compare it with Mark 5, Mark 7, Hebrews 9–10, and 1 John 1.
Do not simply remember what this article says.
Open the Scriptures and examine whether these things are so.
That is the kind of discipleship we want to encourage through Gospel Warrior.
Not shallow religious excitement that disappears after a few seconds.
Not sensational claims that cannot survive biblical examination.
Not guilt-driven spirituality.
But believers who know Jesus Christ, love His Word, recognize false teaching, repent of genuine sin, and grow in grace and truth.
There is room for honest questions here.
There is room for careful study.
There is room for testimonies of grace.
And there is a continuing call to take the Gospel seriously.
Those resources are part of our desire to make biblical learning and spiritual nourishment more accessible.
And there is another way you can help this work continue.

It is voluntary financial support that helps sustain and expand this ministry's work of producing biblical teaching, discipleship materials, encouragement, and resources intended to point people to Christ.
If you are looking for a place to direct part of your Christian giving, you may prayerfully consider Gospel Warrior among the ministries you support.
But I want to be very clear about something important.
The Bible teaches generosity that comes from a willing heart.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — KJV
Not grudgingly.
Not of necessity.
Not under pressure.
Your giving should be thoughtful, willing, and directed toward the glory of God.
It is not the reason to follow Jesus.
And it is certainly not the measure of anyone's faith.
The greater purpose is to help more people discover the truth of God's Word and grow in the knowledge of Jesus Christ.
You can still pray for the ministry.
Read and share the free resources.
Encourage another believer.
Invite someone to study Scripture.
And continue growing in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.
Christ alone is our Savior.
And the Gospel must never be placed behind a financial demand.
That conviction is part of the very truth we want to protect.
Because the message of Gospel Warrior is not that a payment can turn scandal into grace.
It is that Jesus Christ, through His death and resurrection, saves sinners and transforms lives.
Think about the distance we have traveled together.
We began with a verse about a bodily emission.
A man washing.
A period of ritual uncleanness.
A command that seemed strange, uncomfortable, and almost impossible to discuss.
And we discovered something worth remembering.
Not every condition called unclean under the Mosaic Law was a moral sin.
Not every feeling of shame is the voice of God.
Not every outwardly clean person has a pure heart.
And no sinner can cleanse himself from unrighteousness through religious performance.
We need truth.
We need repentance.
We need grace.
We need the blood of Jesus Christ.
We need the Savior who does not confuse human weakness with wickedness, yet never pretends that genuine wickedness is harmless.
The Savior who knows the difference.
The Savior who calls sin by its rightful name.
The Savior who forgives those who turn to Him in faith.
And the Savior who transforms people from the inside out.
So before you leave this article, I want you to remember one final thing.
The man in Leviticus could wash his body and wait until evening.
But the sinner who comes to Jesus finds something infinitely greater than the end of a ceremonial waiting period.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
A new life in Christ.
A hope that reaches beyond the grave.
And a Savior who will never need to offer Himself again.
If you are carrying false guilt, bring your confusion into the light of Scripture.
If you are hiding genuine sin, confess it and turn to Christ.
If you are weary, come to Him.
If you have wandered, hear His call.
And if you have never trusted Jesus Christ, do not mistake knowing religious rules for knowing the Redeemer.
The Gospel is not merely an explanation of what made ancient Israelites ritually unclean.
It is the good news that Jesus Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again, according to the Scriptures.
That is the message of 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
And that is the hope we must never lose.

The deepest scandal was never that a human body could become ceremonially unclean—it was that sinners could stand guilty before a holy God, and the sinless Savior would give His own life to bring them home.
